corrosion-001.question: At 25 °C, the standard electrode potentials are +0.34 V for Cu²⁺/Cu, −0.44 V for Fe²⁺/Fe and −0.76 V for Zn²⁺/Zn. Which of these three metals is thermodynamically the most easily oxidized (most readily becomes a cation)?
choices: Copper
Iron
Zinc
corrosion-001.explanation: The standard electrode potential expresses the equilibrium between a metal and its ions relative to the standard hydrogen electrode at 0 V. The more negative (more active) the value, the stronger the tendency of the metal to give up electrons and become a cation, so of the three, zinc at −0.76 V is the most easily oxidized and copper at +0.34 V is the least (the most noble). Choosing copper reads the sign the wrong way round. Iron (−0.44 V) is more noble than zinc, so it is not as easily oxidized. Note, however, that the standard electrode potential indicates a tendency, not the actual rate of corrosion. Aluminum, for example, is very active at −1.66 V, but resists the atmosphere well thanks to its dense surface oxide film. To evaluate metal combinations in real environments, the ranking of corrosion potentials measured in seawater (the galvanic series) is used.

corrosion-002.question: When local cells form on an iron surface in neutral, aerated water and corrosion proceeds, which reaction mainly occurs at the cathode?
choices: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻
O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
corrosion-002.explanation: Even on the surface of a single metal, inclusions, grain boundaries, strain and nonuniformities in the environment create regions of lower and higher potential, and with the metal itself acting as the wire, many small cells form. These are local cells. At the lower-potential anodes, iron dissolves as Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (the choice giving this equation is the anode reaction), and at the cathodes that accept these electrons, in neutral water, the main reaction is reduction of dissolved oxygen, O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. The Fe²⁺ and OH⁻ produced react and are further oxidized into red rust (FeOOH and others). Hydrogen evolution, 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, is the main reaction in acidic solutions rich in H⁺; in neutral water, H⁺ is scarce at about 10⁻⁷ mol/L, so it does not play the main role.

corrosion-003.question: When the concentration of dissolved oxygen varies from place to place on steel in water, a differential aeration cell forms. Where does corrosion tend to concentrate?
choices: Where the oxygen supply is low (deep in crevices, under deposits and so on)
Where the oxygen supply is high (near the waterline and so on)
An oxygen concentration difference does not create a cell, so the whole surface corrodes almost uniformly
corrosion-003.explanation: Where oxygen is plentifully supplied, the cathodic reaction of oxygen reduction occurs readily and the potential is higher. A cell therefore forms in which the oxygen-poor regions become anodes where iron dissolves, and the oxygen-rich regions become cathodes. This is the differential aeration (oxygen concentration) cell, and corrosion concentrates where oxygen has difficulty reaching: deep in crevices, under deposits, just below the waterline and so on. The choice naming the oxygen-rich regions reverses anode and cathode. An oxygen concentration difference alone creates a potential difference, so the choice saying the whole surface corrodes almost uniformly is also wrong. Inside a crevice, hydrolysis of the dissolved metal ions acidifies the solution and chloride ions also collect, accelerating corrosion further (crevice corrosion). Bolted joints and areas under gaskets are typical sites.

corrosion-004.question: A zinc sacrificial anode is attached to a steel structure in seawater. Treating it as a cell under standard conditions with standard electrode potentials of −0.44 V for Fe²⁺/Fe and −0.76 V for Zn²⁺/Zn, which correctly gives the emf and the metal that dissolves?
choices: About 0.32 V; zinc dissolves and the steel is protected
About 0.32 V; the steel dissolves and the zinc is protected
About 1.20 V; zinc dissolves and the steel is protected
corrosion-004.explanation: The emf is the potential of the cathode side (the more noble iron) minus that of the anode side (the more active zinc): E = −0.44 − (−0.76) = 0.32 V. The active zinc becomes the anode and dissolves as Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻, and the electrons flow into the steel, making it the cathode, so dissolution of the steel is suppressed. This is cathodic protection by sacrificial anodes (the galvanic anode method), used for ship hulls, harbor steel structures and buried pipelines; the anodes are consumed and are replaced periodically. About 1.20 V is the mistake of adding the magnitudes of the two potentials. The choice of about 0.32 V with the steel dissolving reverses noble and active. Actual potentials in seawater differ from standard electrode potentials, but zinc is still more active than steel.

corrosion-005.question: Steel and copper are used in electrical contact in seawater. In which case is galvanic damage to the steel likely to be most severe?
choices: A large steel plate fastened with small copper rivets
A large copper plate fastened with small steel rivets
Regardless of the area ratio, the steel corrodes at the same rate in both
corrosion-005.explanation: When dissimilar metals are in contact, the active steel becomes the anode and the noble copper the cathode, accelerating corrosion of the steel (galvanic corrosion). The amount of oxygen reduced at the cathode is roughly proportional to the cathode area, and the anodic dissolution current equals it, so the corrosion current is set mainly by the cathode area. With a large copper cathode plate and small steel anode rivets, a large current concentrates on a small area, and the rivets corrode severely in a short time. Conversely, with small copper rivets in a large steel plate, the corrosion current is spread over a wide steel surface, so the corrosion rate (per unit area) is small. The choice saying the area ratio has no effect is therefore also wrong. When joining dissimilar metals, the rule is to make the fasteners the more noble metal or to insulate the joint.

corrosion-006.question: What is the main reason stainless steel resists rusting in air and water?
choices: Adding Ni makes the standard electrode potential of the alloy as noble as gold or platinum, so it hardly dissolves
A dense oxide scale several millimeters thick forms on the surface and seals it off from water and oxygen
It contains about 11% or more Cr, forming a passive film a few nanometers thick that re-forms by itself
corrosion-006.explanation: Because stainless steel contains roughly 11% Cr or more (10.5% by the standard definition), a passive film consisting mainly of Cr oxide, only a few nanometers thick, forms on the surface and prevents further dissolution of the metal. What matters is that in environments containing oxygen the film spontaneously re-forms even when scratched. Passivity is therefore readily maintained in oxidizing environments such as nitric acid, but breaks down easily in oxygen-poor environments, chloride-rich environments and reducing acids (such as hydrochloric acid). The potential of the alloy as a whole does not become as noble as gold or platinum; the main role of Ni is to stabilize the austenitic structure. A thick oxide scale several millimeters thick forms by high-temperature oxidation, cracks and spalls easily, and is entirely different from a passive film.

corrosion-007.question: When SUS304 (JIS; AISI 304) is used in chloride-rich seawater, which correctly pairs the localized corrosion likely to occur with a countermeasure?
choices: Uniform corrosion; increase the wall thickness as a corrosion allowance
Pitting corrosion; switch to a Mo-bearing grade such as SUS316
Pitting corrosion; switch to a stainless steel with higher carbon
corrosion-007.explanation: Chloride ions locally break down the passive film at weak points and cause pitting corrosion, in which small holes are dug deeper and deeper. Inside the pit, hydrolysis of the dissolved metal ions acidifies the solution, and chloride ions collect to maintain electrical neutrality, so the corrosion becomes self-accelerating. The large surrounding passive surface acts as the cathode and the bottom of the pit as a small anode, so the pit can advance rapidly to perforation. The countermeasure is to switch to a grade richer in Mo, Cr and N, which strengthen the film (such as SUS316, equivalent to AISI 316, with about 2–3% Mo); the pitting resistance equivalent number calculated from these contents is a guide for selection. Because this is not corrosion that thins the whole surface uniformly, increasing the wall thickness is not an effective countermeasure. More carbon makes Cr carbides form more readily at grain boundaries (sensitization) and actually lowers corrosion resistance.

corrosion-008.question: Which statement about stress corrosion cracking is correct?
choices: It tends to occur where shot peening has introduced compressive residual stress at the surface
It occurs only when the applied stress exceeds the yield stress and the material deforms plastically
It occurs when a susceptible material is under tensile stress in a specific corrosive environment
corrosion-008.explanation: Stress corrosion cracking is the growth of cracks, even at stresses far below the yield stress, when a susceptible material under tensile stress (from external loads or from residual stresses due to welding or working) is exposed to a specific corrosive environment. Classic examples are austenitic stainless steels in hot chloride environments and brass in ammonia-containing environments (season cracking). It is dangerous because the part fractures suddenly with almost no visible corrosion. Removing any one of the three conditions prevents it, so residual stresses are reduced by stress-relief annealing or compressive residual stress is introduced at the surface by shot peening. Compressive stress does not open cracks, so the choice saying it occurs readily where there is compressive residual stress is backward. The choice saying it cannot occur below the yield stress is also wrong.

corrosion-009.question: Which of the following statements about the corrosion protection of steel sheet is correct?
choices: With galvanized (zinc-coated) steel sheet, even if a scratch exposes the steel, the surrounding zinc dissolves first and protects the steel
With tinplate (tin-coated steel sheet), too, if a scratch exposes the steel, the tin dissolves first and protects the steel
Paint prevents corrosion by passing a current through the coating to make the steel the cathode
corrosion-009.explanation: Zinc is more active than steel, so even if the coating is scratched and the steel exposed, the zinc becomes the anode and dissolves, protecting the steel as the cathode (sacrificial protection). Tin, on the other hand, is more noble than steel, so tinplate is protected by the tin layer covering the steel only while it is unscratched; once a scratch exposes the steel, the steel becomes the anode and the large tin surface the cathode, which actually accelerates corrosion of the small exposed area. That is why tinplate is used where scratches are unlikely, such as the inside of cans. Paint works as a barrier that keeps water, oxygen and ions from reaching the steel surface, not by passing a current. Zinc-rich paint, which contains a large amount of zinc powder, does also provide sacrificial protection from the zinc in the coating.

corrosion-010.question: In a steel pipe, a corrosion current in which iron dissolves as Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ flowed at an average of 0.10 A for one year (365 days). Which value is closest to the mass of iron dissolved? Take the molar mass of Fe as 55.85 g/mol and the Faraday constant as 96485 C/mol.
choices: About 0.61 kg
About 0.91 kg
About 1.8 kg
corrosion-010.explanation: From Faraday's law, the dissolved mass is m = ItM/(nF). One year is 365 × 24 × 3600 = 3.15×10⁷ s, so the charge passed is Q = 0.10 × 3.15×10⁷ = 3.15×10⁶ C. Since iron goes to Fe²⁺, n = 2, and m = 3.15×10⁶ × 55.85/(2 × 96485) ≈ 913 g, about 0.91 kg. About 1.8 kg is the mistake of taking the number of electrons as n = 1. About 0.61 kg calculates with n = 3, as if iron went to Fe³⁺, which does not match the reaction given. Even a corrosion current of only 0.10 A loses nearly 1 kg of iron in a year, enough to perforate a pipe if concentrated locally.

corrosion-011.question: When the corrosion current density of iron is uniformly 1.0 µA/cm² over the whole surface, which value is closest to the rate at which the surface recedes? Assume iron dissolves as Fe²⁺, with a molar mass of 55.85 g/mol, a density of 7.87 g/cm³, a Faraday constant of 96485 C/mol, and one year as 3.15×10⁷ s.
choices: About 7.7 µm/year
About 23 µm/year
About 12 µm/year
corrosion-011.explanation: The mass dissolved per unit area per second is iM/(nF) = 1.0×10⁻⁶ × 55.85/(2 × 96485) ≈ 2.9×10⁻¹⁰ g/(cm²·s); dividing by the density of 7.87 g/cm³ gives a recession rate of about 3.7×10⁻¹¹ cm/s. Multiplying by one year gives 3.7×10⁻¹¹ × 3.15×10⁷ ≈ 1.16×10⁻³ cm/year, about 12 µm/year (11.6 µm/year). About 23 µm/year is the mistake of taking n = 1. About 7.7 µm/year calculates with n = 3, as if iron dissolved as Fe³⁺, which does not match the stated conditions. Because current density and corrosion rate are proportional, “1 µA/cm² is about 12 µm/year” for iron is a handy conversion when estimating service life from a corrosion current.

corrosion-012.question: Nickel electroplating is carried out at a current density of 2.0 A/dm² for 30 minutes. Assuming 100% current efficiency, which value is closest to the thickness of the deposit? Take Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni, a molar mass of Ni of 58.69 g/mol, a density of 8.90 g/cm³ and a Faraday constant of 96485 C/mol.
choices: About 12 µm
About 25 µm
About 1.2 mm
corrosion-012.explanation: 2.0 A/dm² is 0.020 A/cm², so the charge passed per cm² in 30 minutes (1800 s) is 0.020 × 1800 = 36 C. The deposited mass is 36 × 58.69/(2 × 96485) ≈ 1.09×10⁻² g/cm², and dividing by the density gives a thickness of 1.09×10⁻²/8.90 ≈ 1.23×10⁻³ cm, about 12 µm (12.3 µm). About 25 µm calculates the two-electron reaction with n = 1. About 1.2 mm mistakes dm² for cm² and calculates with 2.0 A/cm², making it 100 times too large (1 dm² = 100 cm²). In practice, hydrogen evolution and other side reactions bring the current efficiency below 100%, so this value is an upper-bound estimate.
